_comment: Every magnitude that decides an order. A weight, a floor or a ladder
position held as a literal in the module that uses it has no owner and no
recorded reason; here the set is enumerable and each entry says why it
holds its value.
Read at import by contextplane/ranking.py, which refuses an unknown id and
refuses to load at all if this list is empty. scripts/check_governed_magnitudes.py
checks this file directly, without going through that loader -- a gate that
asked the loader whether the loader was happy would agree with it by
construction, including on a change that relaxed it. It is wired into
`make lint`, which is a required check.
This governs the PARAMETERS, not the act of ordering. Detecting 'code that
ranks' is not mechanically closeable -- any comparison produces an order --
so the boundary is stated in contextplane/ranking.py rather than implied.
`coupling` records HOW the consumer is bound to its value, because the two
are not equally strong and pretending otherwise would overstate the
guarantee. `consumed` means the module reads the value from here at import;
changing this file changes behaviour. `pinned` means the module still holds
the value and a test asserts the two agree; changing this file alone turns
the suite red rather than changing behaviour. Pinning is used where the
consumer sits on a path whose churn is not worth the coupling -- the
authority ladder feeds claim adjudication -- and it buys the anti-drift
property without the risk.
`validation` separates two things a registry entry could be asserting.
Registration says a number is owned and has a stated reason. Validation
says somebody checked it predicts, and records who, against what, and with
what result. `grandfathered` says neither, on purpose: every magnitude here
is in-production behaviour brought under governance, and marking it
`validated` would assert a check nobody ran. A registry that cannot express
the difference quietly upgrades unexamined numbers to examined ones.
`requires_validated` is set true by the epic whose feature flag consumes the
magnitude. It is the machine-readable half of the safety ordering: a
consumer that demands validation cannot activate on a grandfathered value.

magnitudes.reason: Capability search fuses three arms. Semantic leads because the query is natural language and the embedding arm is the only one that answers a paraphrase; lexical is the tiebreaker that keeps an exact name from being outranked by a near-synonym; graph is smallest because adjacency is evidence of relatedness, not of relevance to this query. The three sum to 1.0 so a fused score stays comparable across queries.

validation.reason: In-production behaviour brought under governance, not a number anybody checked. These weights have ordered capability search since before the registry existed; recording them makes them owned and reviewable, and claiming they were validated would assert a check nobody ran.

magnitudes.reason: Claim serving fuses two arms and weights semantic higher than capability search does, because a claim is a sentence rather than a name: an exact lexical hit on a claim body is weaker evidence of relevance than it is on an entity name. No graph arm exists here, so the two sum to 1.0.

validation.reason: As above. Governing an existing value is worth doing on its own, and is a different act from establishing that the value predicts well.

magnitudes.reason: Strongest first. Ownership outranks observation because an owner asserting about their own subject is accountable for it; within each, a human assertion outranks an extraction and an extraction outranks an inference, because each step adds a derivation whose error the previous one did not carry. Unattributed is last rather than absent so an unsourced claim still orders deterministically instead of sorting arbitrarily.

validation.reason: An ordering derived from an argument about accountability rather than fitted to outcomes, so there is no held-out result to record. Validating it would mean measuring whether higher-ranked sources are in fact more often right, which is worth doing and has not been done.

magnitudes.reason: What an episode is worth keeping, ordered by how hard the signal is to fake. State change leads because a tool that wrote something changed the world outside the transcript, which no amount of discussion does. Outcome decisiveness is next: an episode that ended in a resolution is the one a later reader needs, and it is read only from the last few events so a long argument cannot inflate it. Human engagement is third and deliberately below both -- a person correcting an agent is strong evidence, but a person being present is not, and the signal cannot tell them apart well enough to outrank an act. Novelty is fourth and is the only term that is not computable at write; it is weighted low because a first observation of a thing that never recurs is noise as often as it is news. Entity density and tool diversity are last because both are proxies for activity rather than for consequence, and a busy session that settled nothing should not outscore a short one that did. The six sum to 1.0, so a salience stays comparable across episodes and across tenants.

validation.reason: Nothing has checked that these weights predict what they claim to. The label they would be validated against -- whether a claim was later retrieved and cited on a succeeding turn -- requires a citation-to-outcome join that does not exist yet, so the honest status is that this is a reasoned ordering and not a measured one. E15-T5 builds the weaker report (retrieval rate per salience bucket) from receipts, which is what a first validation would rest on.

magnitudes.reason: Below this, age stops lowering a claim's confidence. An assertion somebody made, citing evidence that still exists, never becomes less informative than no assertion at all -- decaying to zero would claim it is indistinguishable from an invention. The floor sits inside the bucket whose published meaning is "do not act on this", so a fully-decayed claim stays visible and obviously stale rather than vanishing under a caller's default minimum. It is here rather than in the two modules that use it because it was in both: `confidence.py` and `confidence_decay.py` each held their own 0.10 with their own justifying comment and their own test, so changing one would have left the two paths flooring differently while both suites stayed green. That is the sibling invisibility this registry exists for, found by the first review of ordering sites.

validation.reason: Nothing has checked that 0.10 is the right floor. It is a reasoned position -- it must sit inside the do-not-act bucket and above zero -- and the interval that leaves is wide. Validating it needs evidence about how people actually treat fully-decayed claims, which no harness produces today.

magnitudes.reason: Distinct named things per event above which the entity-density signal saturates. Set at three because the point of the signal is to separate a transcript that talks about specific systems from one that does not, and past a few per turn the difference stops meaning more. Governed because it reorders exactly as a weight does: the salience weights already in this registry are applied to a value this number normalises, so moving the ceiling from 3 to 6 changes every episode's score while every weight stays put. Registering the weights and not their saturation points governed half an arithmetic.

validation.reason: Same position as `salience-weights@1`, and for the same reason: the label a validation would rest on -- whether an episode was later retrieved and cited on a succeeding turn -- needs a citation-to-outcome join that does not exist.

magnitudes.reason: Distinct tools per episode above which the tool-diversity signal saturates, for the same reason as the entity-density ceiling: past a handful, more tools indicate a busy session rather than a more consequential one. Held one higher than the entity ceiling because tool invocations are sparser than named entities in the same transcript, so an equal ceiling would saturate the two signals at different rates of actual activity. Governed for the same reason as its sibling -- it normalises a value the registered salience weights are applied to, so it reorders episodes without any weight changing.

validation.reason: Unvalidated on the same grounds as the other two salience entries. Its relationship to the entity ceiling is reasoned from how often each signal appears, not measured.

magnitudes.reason: The zero-acceptance sample a tenant with no configured sampling policy falls back to: the smallest n with (1 - 0.01)**n <= 0.05, which is 299. A tenant that has configured nothing has not decided that little review is acceptable, so the unconfigured floor is the strictest plan this module derives rather than a lax one -- reading silence as permission is the failure the whole fail-closed rule exists to prevent. Governed because it decides how much of a review queue a human must see before the rest is accepted, which is a budget nobody should be able to change by editing a literal.

validation.reason: Acceptance-sampling arithmetic, not a fitted or measured value. There is no held-out result because it is not a prediction: the number follows from two stated inputs and is reproducible by anybody with a calculator.
validation.derived_from: defect tolerance 0.01, consumer's risk 0.05, zero-acceptance plan (c=0)
validation.derivation: P(accept | p) = (1 - p)**n for a zero-acceptance plan. Requiring P(accept | p=0.01) <= 0.05 gives n >= ln(0.05) / ln(0.99) = 298.07, so the smallest whole n is 299. Exact only for a representative draw: E5's queue is ranked and E5-T4 will let a policy dispose of items without a human, so this is a floor on effort rather than a guarantee about the residue.
